lessons.title: Why we restrain horses and choosing a method
lessons.html:
What is restraint?

Restraint means controlling a horse's movement so that a job can be done safely: a vet examination, an injection, clipping, treating a wound, shoeing or loading. Good restraint protects the horse, the handler and the person doing the job. Bad restraint, or too much force, makes horses frightened and more dangerous the next time.

The rule: least restraint that works

Always start with the gentlest method that will keep everyone safe, and increase only if needed. A calm, well-handled horse often needs only a headcollar and a good handler.

Things to think about before choosing a method

  • The job: a quick brush needs little restraint; stitching a wound needs much more.
  • The horse: age, temperament, training, past experiences. A young, unhandled horse or a stallion needs extra care.
  • Pain: a horse in pain may kick or strike even if it is normally quiet.
  • The place: a quiet, non-slip area with enough room and no sharp objects. Not on concrete that is wet.
  • People: enough trained helpers. Everyone must know the plan and their role.

Methods from least to most restraint

MethodUse
Voice, calm handling, a familiar personMost daily jobs
Headcollar and lead held by a handlerGrooming, examinations
Tied up with a quick-release knotGrooming, tacking up on a quiet horse
Bridle or a lead rope with a chain over the nose (only by trained staff)Leading strong horses
Holding up a forelegStops kicking with the hind leg on the same side during treatment
Skin hold on the neckBrief distraction for an injection
TwitchShort procedures on a difficult horse, by experienced staff
Stocks (crush)Vet procedures, scanning mares
SedationOnly given by or on the instruction of a vet

Your safety

Wear boots, gloves and a hard hat with difficult horses. Stand on the same side as the person working on the horse, near the shoulder, never directly in front or behind. Never wrap a rope around your hand. Have a clear escape route.

lessons.title: Tethering with a quick-release knot
lessons.html:
Why a quick-release knot?

A horse that panics while tied can pull back, fall, or break its headcollar and injure its neck. A quick-release knot holds firmly but can be undone with one pull on the loose end, even when the horse is pulling. Never tie a horse with a knot that tightens and cannot be released.

Where to tie

  • To a loop of baling twine or thin string attached to a strong ring or post. The string breaks if the horse panics, so the horse does not get badly hurt.
  • At about the height of the horse's eye, or higher.
  • With about 50 to 60 cm of rope between the ring and the headcollar: long enough to move the head a little, short enough that the horse cannot get a leg over the rope.
  • Never to a gate, a loose rail, a fence wire or anything that can move or break and be dragged.
  • Never by the reins of a bridle.

Tying the quick-release knot

  1. Pass the end of the lead rope through the string loop.
  2. Hold the end in one hand. Make a loop (a bend) in the loose end.
  3. Lay this loop over the part of the rope going to the horse.
  4. Twist the loop round once or twice and push a second bend of the loose end through the first loop. Do not push the end of the rope through.
  5. Pull the part of the rope going to the horse to tighten the knot.
  6. Test: a pull on the loose end should release the knot at once.

Your instructor will show you this knot. Practise it many times on a post until you can tie it quickly without thinking.

Clever horses

Some horses learn to pull the loose end with their teeth and untie themselves. You can pass the loose end loosely through the loop that is left, but you must remember to pull it out again before releasing.

Safety while tied

  • Never leave a tied horse alone for long.
  • Do not stand or crouch under the rope.
  • If a horse pulls back, step out of the way first, then release the knot from the side.

lessons.title: Restraining techniques
lessons.html:
Holding a horse for someone else

  1. Stand on the same side as the person working, at the horse's shoulder, facing the horse's head.
  2. Hold the lead rope about 30 cm from the headcollar with one hand, with the spare rope folded in the other hand.
  3. Do not tie the horse during vet or farrier work unless you are told to; holding is safer because you can move with the horse.
  4. Keep the horse's head turned slightly towards you; its hindquarters then swing away from you and the worker.
  5. Talk calmly and watch the horse's ears and eyes for warning signs.
  6. If the horse moves, move with it. Do not let go unless you are in danger.

Holding up a foreleg

Lift and hold the foreleg on the same side the worker is on. Most horses cannot kick hard with a hind leg while one foreleg is held. Hold the hoof, not the leg, and be ready to release if the horse falls or struggles hard.

Skin hold

Take a fold of loose skin on the neck in front of the shoulder and squeeze firmly. This distracts the horse for a short moment, for example during an injection.

The twitch

A twitch is a loop of rope on a handle, or a metal clamp, placed on the soft part of the upper lip. It is believed to work by releasing natural calming substances in the body. Use it only:

  • When instructed by your supervisor or the vet, by trained staff
  • For a short time; release it as soon as the job is done
  • Never on the ear or tongue
  • Standing to the side, never in front of the horse

If the horse becomes more upset, remove it and tell the vet.

Stocks

Stocks are a strong frame that holds the horse still. Lead the horse in calmly, close the front and back bars, and stay at the head. Never leave a horse alone in stocks. Never climb into stocks with a horse.

Sedation

If a horse cannot be restrained safely with these methods, stop and call the vet. Only a vet may decide on and give sedatives.

Never

  • Never beat a horse or twist its ear.
  • Never tie legs in a way that can make it fall.

Key points

  • Use the least restraint that keeps everyone safe.
  • Tie to a string loop at eye height with a quick-release knot; never by the reins.
  • Stand on the same side as the worker, at the shoulder.
  • Holding up a foreleg helps stop hind leg kicking.
  • Twitches only by trained staff for a short time; sedation only by a vet.

quiz.question: What is the main rule when choosing a restraint method?

options.text: Use the strongest method every time
Use the least restraint that keeps everyone safe

quiz.question: Why tie a horse to a loop of string instead of directly to the ring?

options.text: The string breaks if the horse panics, so it is less likely to be hurt

quiz.question: How do you test a quick-release knot?

options.text: Pull on the part going to the horse
A pull on the loose end should release it at once

quiz.question: Where should the person holding the horse stand?

options.text: On the same side as the worker, at the shoulder
Directly in front of the horse

quiz.question: Why hold up a foreleg during treatment?

options.text: Most horses cannot kick hard with a hind leg while a foreleg is held
To make the horse lie down

quiz.question: A twitch may be put on a horse's ear.
Only a vet may decide on and give sedatives.
Where should you never tie a horse? (select all that apply)

options.text: To a gate or loose rail
By the reins of a bridle
To a string loop on a strong ring
